messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan is a 19-year-old fast food worker who came to treatment months after a hurricane tore through his town. During the storm he had been in his family’s small house with his mother and younger sister, listening to the wind rise from something strange and distant into a force that seemed to press on the walls from every side. He remembers the lights going out, the rooms turning flat and dark except for brief blue flashes through the windows, and the smell that filled the house as rain forced its way inside—wet wood, mud, damp insulation, and something sour from the flooded kitchen. At the height of it, part of the roof gave way and water came pouring in. He can still picture his mother yelling for them to get low and move to the hallway while debris struck the outside of the house. What stayed with him was not just that he thought they might die, but the feeling that in those minutes the world had become uncontrollable and unsafe.

In the weeks afterward, Ethan found that remembering the storm did not feel like recalling something finished. When it came back, it came back with the same terror, as if his body had not understood that it was over. His memories were mostly images: the sagging ceiling, the dark hallway, water spreading across the floor, his sister crying with her hands over her ears. Sometimes, when his mind touched the event, he could smell the same mix of wet wood and floodwater he had smelled that night, and that sensory jolt made the memory feel present rather than past. Those moments frightened him partly because they seemed to confirm what he had already started to believe about himself: that the storm had changed him in some permanent way, that he was no longer the easygoing, happy person he used to be.

Over time Ethan came to describe himself in harsh, global terms. He had been the one friends joked with, the one who could take things in stride, and now he felt miserable most of the time and alien to himself. He told himself that the person he had become was almost unrecognizable, and he was certain the change was for the worse rather than a phase he might grow out of. Those beliefs shaped how he moved through each day. Because he assumed he could not handle strain the way he once did, he began avoiding anything he thought might be stressful. Before even ordinary interactions, he would rehearse what to say in his head, trying to prevent himself from freezing, sounding strange, or letting other people see how different he felt. He also worked hard to push away thoughts of the hurricane, as if allowing them in would prove that he was damaged beyond repair.

That effort to manage himself narrowed his life. At the restaurant where he worked, the lunch rush became something he dreaded not only because of the pace, but because stress itself had started to feel dangerous. If a customer seemed impatient or a manager called his name sharply from across the kitchen, Ethan would already be running through lines in his head before he answered. He volunteered less for the front counter and tried to keep to repetitive tasks when he could. He avoided conversations in the break room unless he had prepared for them first. The more he organized his day around sidestepping pressure and suppressing reminders of the storm, the more convinced he became that he really had changed for the worse; in his mind, needing all this effort just to get through a shift was evidence that the old Ethan was gone.

His attempts not to think about the hurricane did not loosen its hold. If anything, the memories seemed to hit harder for being fought off. A whiff of bleach mixed with standing water near the mop sink at work, or a flash of rainwater running past the drive-through window during a storm, could pull up vivid pictures and that same wave of terror before he had words for what was happening. Each return of the memory fed his belief that he was permanently damaged and would never be happy in the way he had been before. And because he saw those reactions as proof of what he had become, he doubled down on avoiding stress, rehearsing conversations, and forcing the thoughts away, which only made his world feel smaller and his sense of himself more bleak.

By the time he sought help, Ethan was still showing up to work, but with increasing effort and dread. He had started to worry that if he kept living this way he would lose his job or stop recognizing himself altogether. What finally brought him in was the realization, after a recent rainstorm left him shaken in the stock room by the smell of wet cardboard and cleaning chemicals, that he could not keep outrunning this. He says he wants “to be normal again,” but what frightens him most is that normal may be gone for good.
